newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: SOCCER-ARGENTINE SOCCER PRESIDENT BROUGHT BEFORE CONGRESS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ARGENTINE SOCCER PRESIDENT BROUGHT BEFORE CONGRESS.

text.p: Argentina's Congress spent 90 minutes grilling the president of the country's soccer federation (AFA) on Tuesday over the brawl involving the national team in a World Cup qualifier against Bolivia.
But national team coach Daniel Passerella ignored a request to appear with AFA president Julio Grondona, claiming Congress should be concerned with other issues.

"This is a lesser matter. There are more important things we should be worried with," said Passarella, who instead went to the AFA headquarters where he announced the squad for this month's World Cup qualifier at home to Ecuador.
The game in the Bolivian capital La Paz two weeks ago was held up for 10 minutes as the Argentine players became involved in a fight with members of the Bolivian team bench.
Local riot police intervened to separate brawling players and officials. Earlier, two Argentine players had been sent off.

Congresswoman Beatriz Sampietro, who asked for the hearing, said the matter had become of national concern, especially as Buenos Aires has bid to host the 2004 Olympics and has made the final shortlist of five candidate cities.
"There is a great deal of worry in Congress," she said. "This is a matter of great importance for a country that wants to host the Olympic Games."
Grondona, who gave firm answers and maintained a serious air, answered questions and read part of the report the AFA has sent to world soccer's governing body FIFA.
He was quizzed over a cut to striker Julio Cruz, whose clash with the Bolivian bench began the fight.
Argentines have been worried the team could be accused of faking the injury because Cruz appeared in photos after the game with the left side of his face bleeding.
But television pictures of the fight itself, transmitted in Argentina, showed that during his altercation, he was struck on the other side of the face.
Argentina's neighbours Chile were banned from the 1994 World Cup qualifiers after FIFA judged them guilty in a similar case during a match against Brazil in 1989.

However, Grondona, who did not travel to the game because he was recovering from illness, read a report by team doctor Luis Seveso stating that the cut happened when Cruz banged his face against a table in the dressing room afterwards.
"Seveso is a good person with an excellent record," he added.
